content: The genus Campylobacter consists of Gram-negative, spiral-shaped, microaerophilic bacteria. These organisms are motile, possessing either single or bipolar flagella, and exhibit a curved, rod-like morphology. They are oxidase-positive. Among the species, Campylobacter jejuni is recognized as one of the leading causes of bacterial foodborne illness in many developed nations. At least twelve species of Campylobacter have been implicated in human diseases, with C. jejuni and C. coli being the most prevalent. Additionally, C. fetus is known to cause spontaneous abortions in cattle and sheep and can act as an opportunistic pathogen in humans. The genomes of several Campylobacter species have been sequenced, providing valuable insights into their pathogenic mechanisms. These bacteria possess two flagellin genes, flaA and flaB, arranged in tandem, which are essential for motility. These genes undergo intergenic recombination, contributing to the organism's virulence. Non-motile mutants of Campylobacter are unable to colonize their hosts. Infections caused by Campylobacter, collectively referred to as campylobacteriosis, are typically transmitted through fecal-oral routes, person-to-person sexual contact, or the ingestion of contaminated food or water. The infection often results in inflammatory diarrhea, which may be bloody, and can present with symptoms such as abdominal cramps, fever, and pain. In some cases, the infection may manifest as periodontitis or dysentery. The disease is usually self-limiting, and symptomatic treatment involving fluid and electrolyte replacement is often sufficient. The use of antibiotics in treating Campylobacter infections remains a topic of debate. The most common causative agent of campylobacteriosis is C. jejuni, a spiral or comma-shaped bacterium that is non-pathogenic in its natural hosts, such as cattle, swine, and birds. However, the illness can also be caused by other species, including C. coli (found in cattle, swine, and birds), C. upsaliensis (associated with cats and dogs), and C. lari (commonly found in seabirds). The pathogenic effects of Campylobacter infections are partly due to tissue injury in the gastrointestinal tract, particularly in the jejunum, ileum, and colon. C. jejuni achieves this by invading and destroying epithelial cells. Some strains of C. jejuni produce a cholera-like enterotoxin, which contributes to the watery diarrhea observed in infections. The organism also induces diffuse, bloody, edematous, and exudative enteritis. In rare cases, the infection may be associated with hemolytic uremic syndrome or thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, although the mechanisms underlying these complications are not well understood. Differentiating Campylobacter infections from other causes of viral, bacterial, or parasitic gastroenteritis is essential. Small bowel diarrhea caused by Campylobacter is typically watery and voluminous, with fewer than five white blood cells (WBCs) per high-power field. In contrast, large bowel diarrhea is often mucousy and/or bloody, with lower volume and more than ten WBCs per high-power field. In some cases, the WBC count can reach as high as 1,000, depending on the patient’s immune status. A 3D computer-generated image of a cluster of drug-resistant Campylobacter bacteria, sourced from the Public Health Image Library (PHIL), provides a visual representation of these pathogens.
